Title: International business research that moves Africa
Abstract: The Nachum et al. (J Int Bus Stud 54(5):938–955, 2023) Point article and the Kamoche and Wood (J Int Bus Stud 54(5):956–967, 2023) Counterpoint article each use interesting theory to argue that people-centric mechanisms and indigenous theories of Africa, respectively, offer opportunities for international business (IB) research. Although interesting theory is centered on academic impact, there are other impacts—societal, practical, policy, and educational—that matter to IB scholars of Africa. Focusing on those impacts, and using moving theory , I integrate positivity, history, and impact “turns” into a functional framework that shows how IB scholars interested in Africa can conduct research that addresses the immediate pressing requirements of being—inclusive development, capabilities, and maintenance—that matter to African societies, organizations, and individuals. The expansive framework draws in scholars of the cognate fields of IB to conduct research that prompts change and recognition, is restorative and reformative, and realigns and remodels the practices, knowledge systems, and behaviors of individuals, organizations, and societies. These functions are essential for creating impacts that appeal to leaders, practitioners, policymakers, and educators. As such, the framework aligns with the strategic aim of JIBS to foster research that helps build a better world. L'article Point de Nachum et al. (2023) et l'article Counterpoint de Kamoche et Wood (2023) utilisent tous deux la théorie intéressante afin d’argumenter que les mécanismes centrés sur les personnes et les théories indigènes de l'Afrique offrent respectivement des opportunités pour la recherche en affaires internationales ( International Business - IB). Bien que la théorie intéressante soit centrée sur l'impact académique, il existe d'autres impacts - sociétaux, pratiques, politiques et éducatifs - qui importent aux chercheurs en IB intéressés par l’Afrique. En me concentrant sur ces impacts et en utilisant la théorie du mouvement , j'intègre la positivité, l'histoire et les « tournants » de l'impact dans un cadre fonctionnel lequel montre comment les chercheurs en IB intéressés par l'Afrique peuvent mener des recherches qui répondent aux besoins urgents et immédiats de l'être - le développement inclusif, les capacités et le maintien - qui sont importants pour les sociétés, les organisations et les individus africains. Ce cadre étendu fait appel aux chercheurs des domaines connexes de l'IB pour mener des recherches qui incitent au changement et à la reconnaissance, qui sont réparatrices et réformatrices, et qui réalignent et remodèlent les pratiques, les systèmes de connaissances et les comportements des individus, des organisations et des sociétés. Ces fonctions sont essentielles pour créer des impacts qui intéressent les dirigeants, les praticiens, les décideurs politiques et les éducateurs. En tant que tel, le cadre s'aligne sur l'objectif stratégique de la revue JIBS qui est de favoriser la recherche susceptible de contribuer à construire un monde meilleur. El artículo que presenta el Punto de Nachum et al. (2023) y el artículo donde está el Contrapunto por Kamoche y Wood (2023) utilizan cada uno teorías interesantes para argumentar que los mecanismos centrados en las personas y las teorías autóctonas de África, respectivamente, ofrecen oportunidades para la investigación sobre negocios internacionales (IB por sus iniciales en inglés). Aunque la teoría interesante se centra en el impacto académico, hay otros impactos -sociales, prácticos, políticos y educativos- que son importantes para los estudiosos de los negocios internacionales en África. Centrándome en esos impactos, y utilizando la teoría en movimiento , integro la positividad, la historia y los “giros” del impacto en un marco funcional que muestra cómo los académicos de Negocios Internacionales interesados en África pueden llevar a cabo investigaciones que aborden los requisitos apremiantes inmediatos

Title: The convention on tax mutual administrative assistance and divestment: Evidence from China
Authors: Xiaoning Song, Jiayan Yan, Guilong Cai, Huimin (Amy) Chen
Abstract: Varios instrumentos políticos se han usado para combatir la evasión de impuestos internacionales por parte de las corporaciones multinacionales (MNCs por sus iniciales en inglés, con un enfoque en declaración del impuesto de sociedades. Sin embargo, la sola declaración del impuesto de sociedades a las autoridades fiscales no basta para resolver el problema. El Convenio sobre Asistencia Administrativa Mutua en Materia Fiscal (el Convenio) va más allá de la divulgación de información fiscal, ya que ofrece asistencia administrativa fiscal internacional directa y busca reforzar la aplicación de la legislación fiscal por parte de los gobiernos. Intrigados por la singularidad del Convenio, examinamos su efecto sobre la evasión fiscal de las multinacionales chinas, en particular sus inversiones en jurisdicciones con paraísos fiscales. Suponemos que las multinacionales chinas, previendo una aplicación más estricta de la legislación fiscal tras la Convención, podrían reducir su evasión fiscal y desinvertir en paraísos fiscales. Usando la entrada gradual de China y otros países en la Convención, encontramos que después de la Convención, las multinacionales chinas tienden a desinvertir en paraísos fiscales, observándose un efecto más fuerte en las multinacionales cuyas casas matrices se encuentran en regiones con una débil aplicación de la legislación fiscal. Además, observamos un descenso de la agresividad fiscal general tras la Convención. Nuestros resultados resaltan el efecto sancionatorio del Convenio, amplían la literatura sobre la evasión fiscal en la colaboración internacional y ayudan a la OCDE y a otros reguladores internacionales a entender mejor su impacto en los países con una capacidad administrativa limitada. 为了遏制跨国公司（MNC）的国际避税活动，各国采取各种政策手段，政策的重点是加强公司税务信息披露。然而，仅向税务机关披露税务信息不足以解决这个问题。《多边税收征管互助公约》（简称《公约》）超越了信息披露，其 特点是直接的国际税务行政协助，旨在提升各国政府的税务执法能力。为了探讨《公约》的独特作用，我们研究其对 中国跨国公司避税行为的影响，特别是对其在“避税天堂”投资的影响。我们预期，中国签署《公约》后，中国跨国公 司预见到未来税收执法的加强，可能会减少避税行为，并减少在“避税天堂”的投资。基于多期DID方法，实证研究发 现，中国《公约》签署后，中国跨国公司倾向于从“避税天堂”撤资。那些母公司位于税收执法薄弱地区的跨国公司，其撤资行为更为明显。此外，中国签署《公约》后，跨国公司的税务筹划激进度有所下降。本研究凸显了《公约》 遏制跨国公司避税中的重要作用，拓展了相关避税研究文献，并为经合组织和其他国际组织更好地理解《公约》对税 收执法能力薄弱国家的影响提供了启示。 Various policy instruments have been employed to combat international tax avoidance by multinational corporations (MNCs), with a focus on corporate tax disclosure. However, corporate tax disclosure to tax authorities alone is insufficient to address the issue. The Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters (the Convention) goes beyond tax disclosure by featuring direct international tax administrative assistance and aiming to strengthen governments’ tax enforcement. Intrigued by the uniqueness of the Convention, we examine its effect on Chinese MNCs’ tax avoidance, particularly their investments in tax-haven jurisdictions. We conjecture that Chinese MNCs, anticipating strengthened tax enforcement after the Convention, may reduce tax-avoidance behavior and divest from tax havens. Using the staggered entry of China and other countries into the Convention, we find that after the Convention, Chinese MNCs tend to divest from tax havens, with a stronger effect observed in MNCs whose parent firms are in regions with weak tax enforcement. Additionally, we observe a decline in overall tax aggressiveness following the Convention. Our findings highlight the Convention’s disciplining effect, extend the tax avoidance literature on international collaboration, and help the OECD and other international regulators better understand its impact on countries with limited administrative capacity. Vários instrumentos de política foram empregados para combater a elisão fiscal internacional por corporações multinacionais (MNCs), com foco na divulgação fiscal corporativa. No entanto, a divulgação fiscal corporativa apenas para autoridades fiscais é insuficiente para abordar a questão. Title: Product market bonding and cross-listings: evidence from global competition law reforms
Authors: Albert Tsang, Kun Tracy Wang, Nathan Zhenghang Zhu
Abstract: Propomos e testamos empiricamente um motivo no mercado de produtos para dupla listagem, postulando que a competição intensificada nos mercados domésticos incentiva empresas a listar duplamente seus títulos como uma resposta estratégica para mitigar o impacto adverso da competição aumentada em casa. Utilizando um conjunto de dados abrangente de dupla listagem coletado manualmente, cobrindo 56 países de origem e 45 países anfitriões de dupla listagem, juntamente com uma nova métrica para reformas na legislação de concorrência que intensificam a concorrência no mercado de produtos nos países de origem das empresas, nosso estudo fornece evidências robustas que apoiam essa hipótese. Descobrimos que as empresas têm mais probabilidade de listar duplamente seus títulos após a implementação de reformas na legislação de concorrência em seus países de origem. Análises adicionais sugerem que a dupla listagem facilita que empresas adquiram uma compreensão mais profunda dos mercados de produtos estrangeiros, sinalizando seu compromisso em oferecer produtos superiores e aumentando a conscientização sobre produto/marca em países estrangeiros. É importante ressaltar que demonstramos que a dupla listagem influencia positivamente vendas no exterior, sublinhando sua eficácia como uma ferramenta estratégica para fortalecer a presença de uma empresa em mercados de produtos estrangeiros em meio à concorrência doméstica aumentada. No geral, nosso estudo identifica um motivo estratégico do mercado de produtos para dupla listagem e oferece insights acionáveis para empresas melhorarem seu posicionamento de mercado em um ambiente global cada vez mais competitivo. In recent years, the phenomenon of "cross-listing" (listing a company's shares on a foreign stock exchange in addition to its home country's exchange) has become increasingly common. This trend has sparked interest among researchers trying to understand why companies take this step. While some theories suggest that cross-listing helps companies access more capital or signal strong corporate governance (the system by which companies are directed and controlled), there's a puzzle: even firms that are not in need of capital often cross-list. This suggests that there might be other reasons for cross-listing that existing theories don't fully explain. This study introduces the idea of "product market bonding" as a new reason for cross-listing. The researchers propose that companies might cross-list in foreign markets as a strategic move to strengthen their position in those markets, especially when their home markets become more competitive due to stricter competition laws (rules designed to prevent anti-competitive practices and encourage fair competition). When these laws get tougher, companies might find it harder to maintain their market share and profits at home, so they look to foreign markets for growth. To test this theory, the researchers used a dataset that includes cross-listing information from 56 home countries and 45 host countries. They focused on how changes in competition laws in a company's home country influenced its decision to cross-list. The study is observational and uses a method called "difference-in-differences" (a statistical technique used to determine the effect of a treatment by comparing the changes in outcomes over time between a treatment group and a control group) to compare the behavior of firms before and after competition law reforms. The results showed that firms in countries with new competition law reforms were more likely to cross-list their securities abroad. This supports the idea that companies use cross-listing as a way to bond with foreign product markets and counteract the challenges posed by increased competition at home. Title: How to avoid a desk reject: do’s and don’ts
Publisher Correction: Forgotten globalizing actors: towards an understanding of the range of individuals involved in global norm formation in multinational companies
Authors: Tony Edwards, Kyoungmi Kim, Phil Almond, Philipp Kern, Olga Tregaskis, Ling Eleanor Zhang

Title: Forgotten globalizing actors: towards an understanding of the range of individuals involved in global norm formation in multinational companies
Authors: Tony Edwards, Kyoungmi Kim, Phil Almond, Philipp Kern, Olga Tregaskis, Ling Eleanor Zhang
Abstract: Abstract While there is substantial literature on global mobility, roles in the global integration of multinationals are not limited to internationally mobile staff. We focus on ‘globalizing actors’, defined as those within multinationals who are involved in global norm-making. Using interview-based qualitative data, we categorize individuals’ involvement in global norm-making according to the function within norm formation in which they are involved, their source of influence, and their geographical and organizational reach. We identify nine distinct types of globalizing actors. We demonstrate that many individuals play important roles in global norm-making without having formal hierarchical authority or being globally mobile. Our approach draws attention to the ways in which many globalizing actors use ‘social skill’ to further their aims. Our categorization of such ‘forgotten globalizing actors’ facilitates future research by allowing a fuller understanding of the ways in which individuals across multinationals contribute to global integration.

Title: Expatriates’ boundary-spanning: double-edged effects in multinational enterprises
Authors: Ting Liu, Tomoki Sekiguchi, Jiayin Qin, Ya Xi Shen
Abstract: Abstract Expatriates typically perform boundary-spanning to address challenges related to functional, linguistic, and cultural variations within multinational enterprises (MNEs), which in turn influences their relationships with host-country employees. Integrating social capital and role theory perspectives, this study explores the relational dynamics between expatriates and host-country employees by developing a novel theoretical framework that examines the double-edged effects of expatriates’ boundary-spanning. We propose that expatriates’ boundary-spanning nurtures mutual trust between expatriates and host-country employees, further facilitating expatriates’ identification with subsidiaries and host-country employees’ identification with MNEs. On the other hand, we propose that boundary-spanning increases expatriates’ role stressors, causing expatriates’ emotional exhaustion and outgroup categorization by host-country employees. We further categorize expatriates’ boundary-spanning into three types (functional, linguistic, and cultural) and theorize about their varying effects on the cognitive and affective bases of mutual trust and on role stressors. With data from 177 expatriate–host-country coworker dyads in Chinese MNEs, our double-edged framework is generally supported. Our findings suggest that cultural boundary-spanning exhibits the strongest double-edged effect, while functional boundary-spanning shows asymmetric effects, with negative outcomes surpassing positive ones, and linguistic boundary-spanning demonstrates the weakest effect. This study offers realistic and comprehensive insights into expatriates’ boundary-spanning, particularly in expatriate–host-country employee relationships.

Title: Publisher Correction: The impacts of structural configurations on expatriates’ organizational commitment and assignment completion intention
Authors: Riki Takeuchi, Jiatao Li, Hwayoung Kim, Jeffrey P. Shay

Title: The impacts of structural configurations on expatriates’ organizational commitment and assignment completion intention
Authors: Riki Takeuchi, Jiatao Li, Hwayoung Kim, Jeffrey P. Shay
Abstract: 全球员工流动性是跨国企业 (MNE) 的一个重要关注点, 因为此类人员是MNE重要的战略人力资本资源。确保外派人员 (全球流动员工的一种) 保持高度的组织承诺和任务完成意愿 (对国际职位的“依恋”) 是MNE人力资源管理的关键考虑因素。然而, 我们对结构配置 (权力下放、正规化和全球知识整合) – – MNE为控制和协调外国子公司而制定的做法 – – 如何影响外派人员在国际任务期间的依恋关系的了解非常有限。我们通过研究结构配置对外派管理者结果的影响来解决这个研究问题。我们利用从 9 家美国全球连锁酒店雇用的 192 名外派总经理那里获得的调查数据, 提出并检验了一组假设。我们发现, 这三种结构特征创造了不同的配置, 其在保留外派人员依恋结果方面的有效性有所不同。我们的研究结果突出了研究结构特征配置的重要性, 这强调了管理MNE外派经理的困难, 并提供了对与良好管理他们所需的结构配置相关的复杂性的进一步见解。 Mobilidade global de funcionários é uma preocupação crucial para empresas multinacionais (MNEs), já que tais indivíduos são críticos recursos estratégicos de capital humano para MNEs. Garantir que expatriados, um tipo de funcionário com mobilidade global, mantenham um elevado comprometimento organizacional e uma intenção de conclusão de tarefas (“ligação” à designação internacional) são considerações críticas para a gestão de recursos humanos de MNEs. No entanto, temos uma compreensão muito limitada de como as configurações de estruturas (descentralização, formalização e integração global do conhecimento) – práticas implementadas para controlar e coordenar subsidiárias estrangeiras por MNEs – influenciam ligações de expatriados durante missões internacionais. Abordamos esta questão de pesquisa examinando o impacto de configurações estruturais nos resultados dos gestores expatriados. Desenvolvemos e testamos um conjunto de hipóteses utilizando dados de pesquisas obtidos de 192 gerentes gerais expatriados empregados por nove cadeias hoteleiras globais americanas. Descobrimos que estas três características estruturais criam várias configurações que diferem na sua eficácia na manutenção dos resultados de apego de expatriados. As nossas conclusões destacam a importância de examinar configurações das características estruturais, o que sublinha as dificuldades em gerenciar gestores expatriados para MNEs, bem como fornecer insights adicionais sobre as complexidades associadas às configurações estruturais necessárias para bem gerenciá-las. Global employee mobility is a very important concern for multinational enterprises (MNEs), as such individuals are critical strategic human capital resources for MNEs. Ensuring that expatriates (one type of globally mobile employees) maintain high organizational commitment and assignment completion intentions (“attachment” to international posting) is a critical consideration for MNEs’ human resources management. However, we have a very limited understanding of how the configurations of structures (decentralization, formalization, and global knowledge integration) – practices set in place to control and coordinate foreign subsidiaries by MNEs – influence expatriates’ attachments during international assignments. We address this research question by adopting the structural contingency theory and extending it to examine the impact of structural configurations on expatriate managers’ outcomes. We develop and test a set of hypotheses using survey data obtained from 192 expatriate general managers employed by nine American global hotel chains. We find that these three structural characteristics create various configurations differing in their effectiveness in retaining expatriates’ attachment outcomes. Our findings highlight the importance of examining configurations of structural characteristics, which underscores the difficulties of managing expatriate managers for MNEs as well as providing further insights into the complexities associated with structural configurations necessary to manage them well. Garantizar que los expatriados, un tipo de empleados globales móviles, mantienen un alto compromiso organizacional y de intención de finalizar la asignación (“acoplamiento” a la asignación internacional) son condiciones críticas para la gestión de recursos humanos. Title: Foreign-origin managers and FDI location choice
Authors: Massimiliano Coda Zabetta, Ernest Miguelez, Francesco Lissoni, Sarah Hegarty
Abstract: Abstract Building upon the upper echelons theory of organizations as applied to internationalization strategies, we investigate the impact of foreign-origin top management team (TMT) members on their companies’ location choice. We propose that a manager-from-target effect may exist, by which a manager’s knowledge of their country of origin increases the likelihood of choosing that country as a target. We expect it to be stronger for acquisitions than for greenfield investments, the inputs of foreign-origin managers being more relevant in the first case. Based on a large sample of foreign direct investment from 2013 to 2019, and using name analysis to identify TMT members’ origins, we find that the effect is present in both establishment modes but larger and more robust for acquisitions. It is also larger in companies with less diverse TMTs, for which targeting one manager’s country of origin instead of others’ may be less likely to cause conflict. Future research should explore whether investments in locations suggested by managers from the target country outperform others. If this is the case, it implies that recruiting foreign-origin top managers can improve a company’s internationalization strategy via better location choices.

Title: Beyond global mobility: how human capital shapes the MNE in the 21st century
Authors: Dana Minbaeva, Rajneesh Narula, Anupama Phene, Stacey Fitzsimmons
Abstract: A mobilidade global de pessoas transformou a forma como empresas multinacionais (MNEs) gerenciam e se beneficiam de múltiplos locais. Examinamos a mudança de limites locacionais de capital humano com a globalização e como isso impactou a competitividade de MNEs. O uso crescente da quase-internalização por meio da dependência ativa de cadeias de valor globais e terceirização alterou a maneira como MNEs organizam suas atividades espacialmente para otimizar seu acesso ao capital humano, uma importante fonte de vantagens de propriedade. Identificamos áreas para pesquisas futuras, incluindo novas estratégias para gerenciar recursos humanos usando essas novas formas de governança transfronteiriça. Coletivamente, os artigos desta edição especial fornecem insights sobre como MNEs podem alavancar o movimento e a reorganização de seu capital humano para aprimorar suas capacidades únicas e ter sucesso em negócios internacionais. Globalization has greatly influenced international business and migration (movement of people across borders) over the past century. Migration affects a nation's human capital (skills and knowledge possessed by individuals), which is vital for economic competitiveness. However, the societal and business impacts of migration are still debated. This study explores how multinational enterprises (MNEs, companies operating in multiple countries) leverage global mobility to enhance performance. It examines how MNEs strategically use human capital mobility to optimize operations and gain competitive advantages. The research focuses on the role of human capital mobility in MNEs, investigating how they utilize this mobility to access knowledge and skills across various locations. The study highlights the importance of understanding the relationship between global mobility and MNE performance. Various methods, including literature analysis and case studies, are used to explore this relationship. The study emphasizes the need for MNEs to adapt to changing global mobility patterns to remain competitive. Findings show that MNEs benefit from global mobility by accessing diverse talent pools and knowledge sources, enhancing their ability to innovate and compete globally. MNEs strategically relocate employees to optimize operations and access skilled workers. The study concludes that MNEs actively shape global mobility patterns by seeking human capital that aligns with their needs. This research advances the understanding of how MNEs leverage global mobility to enhance competitiveness. It underscores the importance of human capital mobility in driving MNE performance and suggests that MNEs should continue adapting to changing global mobility trends. The findings have significant implications for policymakers and business leaders. Policymakers should consider migration policies' impact on MNEs and their ability to access skilled workers. Business leaders should develop strategies to attract and retain global talent. Future research could explore the impact of digital platforms and remote work on global mobility and MNE performance. Understanding these dynamics will help MNEs navigate the complexities of global mobility and maintain a competitive edge in an increasingly interconnected world. Title: The value of theory- and evidence-based intellectual dialogue on foundational elements of the IB field
JIBS reflections: rare events/outliers, grand challenges, and managerial interaction
Research handbook on international corporate social responsibility
Regulatory actions and reputation spillovers: investor reactions to Foreign Corrupt Practices Act violations
Authors: Seung-Hyun Lee, Jisun Yu, Jinsil Kim
Abstract: This study examines reputational penalty spillovers in the context of multinational enterprises’ (MNE) Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) violations. We focus on investor reactions to unaccused industry bystander MNEs upon two FCPA regulatory events: investigation and enforcement. Expanding on the notion of categorization, we theorize that unaccused bystander MNEs would experience reputation spillover penalties in the investigation stage due to investors’ similarity-based categorization. In the enforcement stage, investors focus more on individual firm traits and no longer rely on similarity-based categorization in their evaluation, resulting in penalties isolated to the focal MNE and competitive benefits to bystander MNEs. Additionally, due to causal-based categorization, these investor reactions would be further influenced by whether the bystander MNEs had subsidiaries in the host country where the bribery had occurred, as well as the level of host-country corruption. We test these arguments using event study methods involving US-listed bystander MNEs upon 190 FCPA regulatory events from 1998 to 2021 and find support for most of our hypotheses. This study provides more nuanced theoretical underpinnings for reputation spillovers and highlights social evaluation aspects in studying MNE corruption and other socially irresponsible practices. Este estudio examina los efectos indirectos de las sanciones en la reputación en el contexto de las violaciones a la Ley de Prácticas Corruptas en el Extranjero (FCPA por sus siglas en inglés) por parte de empresas multinacionales (EMN). Nos enfocamos en las reacciones de los inversionistas ante las multinacionales no acusadas que actúan como espectadoras en dos eventos regulatorios de la Ley de Prácticas Corruptas en el Extranjero: la investigación y la aplicación de sanciones. Ampliando la noción de categorización, planteamos que las multinacionales espectadoras no acusadas experimentarían penalizaciones indirectas en su reputación durante la fase de investigación debido a la categorización basada en similitudes que hacen los inversionistas. En la fase de aplicación de sanciones, los inversionistas se concentran más en las características individuales de la empresa y ya no se basan en la categorización por similitudes en su evaluación, lo que resulta en una penalización aislada para la multinacional implicada y en beneficios competitivos para las multinacionales espectadoras. Además, debido a la categorización basada en causalidad, estas reacciones de los inversionistas se verían aún más influenciadas por el hecho de que las multinacionales espectadoras tuvieran filiales en el país anfitrión donde ocurrió el soborno, así como por el nivel de corrupción del país anfitrión. Probamos estos argumentos utilizando métodos de estudio de eventos que involucran multinacionales espectadoras que cotizan en Estados Unidos en 190 eventos regulatorios de la Ley de Prácticas Corruptas en el Extranjero entre 1998 y 2021, y encontramos respaldo para la mayoría de nuestras hipótesis. Este estudio proporciona fundamentos teóricos más matizados sobre los efectos indirectos en la reputación y destaca los aspectos de evaluación social en el estudio de la corrupción de las multinacionales y otras prácticas socialmente irresponsables. 本研究探讨了跨国企业 (MNE) 违反《美国海外反腐败法》(FCPA) 的情境下的声誉处罚溢出效应。 我们重点关注投资者对未受到指控的行业旁观者MNE在两项FCPA监管事件（调查和执法）中的反应。 我们扩展了分类概念， 认为由于投资者基于相似性的分类， 未受到指控的旁观者MNE将在调查阶段遭受声誉溢出惩罚。在执法阶段， 投资者更多地关注单个企业的特征， 而不再依赖基于相似性的分类进行评估， 从而导致所关注的MNE被孤立处罚， 而旁观者MNE则获得竞争优势。 此外， 由于基于因果关系的分类， 这些投资者的反应将进一步受到旁观者MNE在行贿发生所在国是否设有子公司以及东道国腐败程度的影响。我们使用涉及美国上市的旁观者MNE的事件研究方法， 对 1998 至 2021 年间发生的 190 起 FCPA 监管事件检验了这些论点， 并找到了对我们大多数假设的支持。这项研究为声誉溢出提供了更细微的理论基础， 并强调了研究MNE腐败和其它不负责任的社会行为时的社会评价方面。 Cette recherche examine les répercussions des pénalités de réputation dans le contexte des violations de la loi sur les pratiques de corruption à l'étranger (Foreign Corrupt Practices Act - FCPA) commises par les entreprises multinationales (Multinatio

Title: Restrictive immigration policies and MNE innovation
Authors: Deepak Nayak, Solon Moreira, Ram Mudambi
Abstract: Abstract High-skill migrant workers significantly contribute to advanced economies by directly generating knowledge-intensive assets and serving as bridges to knowledge in their origin countries. However, rising populist sentiment has led to increased immigration restrictions in wealthy economies like the U.S. and the European Union. This study examines the impact of the 2004 H-1B visa cap reduction on U.S.-based multinational enterprises (MNEs). We use a sample of 371,856 patents assigned to 707 U.S.-based MNEs. We find that post-shock, MNEs increased the geographic dispersion of their global R&D workforce, rather than replacing foreigners with local American workers. Despite this, the firms experienced a decline in innovation performance, likely due to elevated coordination challenges. Interestingly, sectors relying more on codified knowledge demonstrated increased R&D team dispersion with less impact on innovation. This suggests that the geographic proximity of innovation teams is crucial for tacit knowledge-intensive sectors. These findings highlight the complex consequences of immigration restrictions and suggest boundary conditions on the effectiveness of work-from-anywhere models in knowledge-intensive industries.

Title: The boundaries of the law: can US private enforcement discipline foreign firms?
Authors: Massimo Massa, Xiaoqiao Wang, Bohui Zhang, Hong Zhang
Abstract: In recent years, the global financial landscape has seen a growing interest in how legal systems, particularly in the United States, can influence financial markets beyond their own borders. While it is well known that legal institutions within a country play a crucial role in protecting shareholders and ensuring market efficiency, there has been less clarity on whether these effects can extend internationally. This study delves into the potential global reach of US class action lawsuits (lawsuits filed by a group of people with similar grievances) and their impact on the efficiency of financial markets in other countries. The research focuses on class action lawsuits because they are a key mechanism for protecting shareholder interests in the US. These lawsuits can have significant consequences for the firms involved, often leading to substantial financial losses. The study examines whether the effects of such lawsuits against companies listed in the US can spill over to similar companies in the same industry but based in other countries, which are not directly subject to US jurisdiction (legal authority). The researchers constructed a dataset of 10,804 pairs of firms from around the world, covering the period from 1994 to 2019. Each pair included a "treated" firm (a non-US peer of a US-listed foreign firm targeted by a class action lawsuit) and a "control" firm (a matched non-US firm in the same country but a different industry). The study used event study methodology (a statistical method to assess the impact of an event on the value of a firm) and difference-in-difference analysis (a statistical technique to determine the effect of a treatment) to compare the valuation and corporate policies of treated and control firms before and after the lawsuits. The results showed that US class action lawsuits against US-listed foreign firms caused a negative spillover effect on the valuation of similar firms in the same industry but based in the home country of the targeted firm. This suggests that the influence of US legal institutions can indeed reach beyond national borders, affecting firms globally. The study also identified two channels through which this impact could occur: the sharing of information through financial markets and the potential for policy coordination (alignment of policies) between countries. In conclusion, the research provides evidence that US class action lawsuits have a disciplining effect on non-US firms, influencing their valuation and prompting them to improve their corporate policies. This finding has significant implications for the understanding of legal institutions' role in financial globalization and suggests that the effects of US legal actions can be far-reaching, potentially shaping corporate behavior worldwide. This text was initially drafted using artificial intelligence, then reviewed by the author(s) to ensure accuracy. Existing studies tend to focus on how a legal system reinforces the efficiency of its domestic firms or foreign companies that are subject to its domestic jurisdiction (e.g., via cross-listing). Our study provides critical normative implications in the era of financial globalization by showing that the influence of a country’s legal institutions extend beyond its territorial boundaries. We examine whether US shareholder-initiated class action lawsuits can discipline non-US firms. Using an international sample of firms over the period 1994–2019, we find that a US class action lawsuit against a non-US firm cross-listed in the US negatively affects the value of its non-US-listed industry peers. The effect is robust in both event-based analyses for short-term market reaction and stacked difference-in-difference analyses for long-term valuation. We uncover two economic mechanisms underlying this effect: information sharing and policy coordination between the US and the non-US firm’s home country. Title: Alternative finance in the international business context: a review and future research
Abstract: Abstract Firms increasingly rely on alternative finance (AF) in addition to banks and equity markets, and its usage across countries differs significantly. We conceptualize AF as financing that operates within social, business, and virtual networks that generate informational, collateral, and incentive advantages compared to finance relying on traditional financial intermediaries. Examples of AF include family loans, microfinance, trade credit, community credit cooperatives, person-to-person (P2P), and crowdfunding. While AF is not a new phenomenon, technological development continues to facilitate its increasing prominence. We review the evolution of AF theories, summarize key empirical findings, and describe how AF intersects with international business (IB) research. Specifically, we review how AF feeds into the analysis of comparative financial systems, financial development, comparative corporate governance, and national culture. We conclude that AF has shaped comparative research in IB in important ways, but cross-border research in IB has hardly considered the role of AF. Globalization and technological development and adoption in the financial industry generate rich fields where AF and IB intersect; these have yet to be understood. We describe how IB research, specifically addressing the cross-border dimension, could benefit from integrating insights from AF research, and propose approaches to integrate theories on AF, IB, and internationalization.

Title: Dynamic capabilities framework and its transformative contributions
Authors: S. Tamer Cavusgil, Seyda Z. Deligonul
Abstract: Capacidades dinâmicos referem-se à capacidade de uma organização de integrar, construir e reconfigurar competências internas e externas para lidar com um ambiente em rápido desenvolvimento. Em seu altamente influente artigo do JIBS de 2014, David Teece fornece uma explicação holística de como empresas podem: obter vantagem competitiva sustentada, ajustar e preservar superior desempenho e adaptar-se a ambientes em mudança. O artigo, juntamente com relacionadas contribuições de Teece, é notável na medida em que nos levou a repensar e reformular nosso entendimento convencional sobre mercados, estratégia, vantagem competitiva e a empresa. Neste comentário, refletimos sobre as contribuições transformadoras do artigo. Argumentamos que o modelo de capacidades dinâmicas fornece uma base para teorizar e desenvolver uma lógica coerente que orienta o desenvolvimento da teoria. Les capacités dynamiques désignent l’aptitude d’une organisation à intégrer, construire et reconfigurer des compétences internes et externes pour faire face à un environnement qui évolue rapidement. Dans son article très influent publié dans la revue JIBS en 2014, David Teece apporte une explication holistique de la manière dont les entreprises peuvent : obtenir un avantage concurrentiel durable, ajuster et préserver des performances supérieures, et s’adapter à des environnements changeants. L’article, ainsi que les contributions connexes de Teece, est remarquable dans la mesure où il nous a amenés à repenser et à recadrer notre compréhension conventionnelle des marchés, de la stratégie, de l’avantage concurrentiel et de l’entreprise. Dans ce commentaire, nous réfléchissons aux contributions transformatrices de l’article. Nous argumentons que la perspective des capacités dynamiques fournit une base pour la théorisation et le développement d’une logique cohérente qui guide l’élaboration de la théorie. In today’s fast-paced global market, multinational enterprises (MNEs, companies operating in multiple countries) need to be agile and adaptable to stay competitive. This study explores the concept of dynamic capabilities (skills and processes enabling firms to integrate, build, and reconfigure resources to adapt to changing environments). Unlike operational capabilities, which focus on maintaining current operations, dynamic capabilities help firms innovate and respond to new challenges. The research highlights the importance of these capabilities for MNEs, especially in the face of nationalism (preference for domestic over foreign products), market instability, and cultural differences. The study draws on David Teece’s influential work on dynamic capabilities, which has gained significant attention across various disciplines. This study reflects on the dynamic capabilities framework (DCF, a structured approach to understanding dynamic capabilities) and its implications for international business and MNEs. It is not a review of the literature but rather an exploration of how the DCF emerged as a distinct framework. The research differentiates dynamic capabilities from ordinary capabilities and addresses criticisms of the DCF. It examines the early development of the framework, linking it to behavioral theory (study of how psychological factors affect decision-making), resource-based view (RBV, a management tool for identifying strategic resources), and transaction cost economics (study of costs incurred in making an economic exchange). The study emphasizes the role of learning in dynamic capabilities, highlighting how they revolutionize traditional perceptions of organizational learning. The research also discusses how the DCF leads to a reconceptualization of markets, strategy, competitive advantage, and the nature of the firm. The results of this study underscore the transformative impact of dynamic capabilities on MNEs. The research concludes that dynamic capabilities are essential for MNEs to navigate and shape global markets. They enable firms to balance stability

Title: Theories of firms and the emergence of multinational enterprises: the organizational and managerial implications of solving transactional problems versus creating exchange value
Authors: Jay B. Barney, Ilze Kivleniece, Anita M. McGahan
Abstract: Teece (2014) identifica duas teorias do aparecimento de empresas multinacionais (MNEs) – uma que se concentra em como MNEs solucionam problemas transacionais que podem surgir nas trocas de mercado e outra que se concentra em como MNEs facilitam a criação de valor econômico que é difícil de realizar por meio de trocas de mercado – e sugere que ambas as teorias são importantes para entender o aparecimento de MNEs. No entanto, as implicações organizacionais e gerenciais dessas duas teorias são bem distintas. MNEs que resolvem dificuldades transacionais são tipicamente de natureza hierárquica, em que gerentes seniores exercem poder hierárquico gerencial para orientar subordinados, limites da empresa são bem definidos e o comportamento de subordinados é monitorado para minimizar oportunismo. MNEs que criam valor econômico são tipicamente menos hierárquicas, promovem a criação de relações de cooperação entre stakeholders para facilitar investimentos coespecializados, têm fronteiras menos bem definidas e reduzem a ameaça de oportunismo por garantir que stakeholders ganhem ao dar continuidade nessa troca do que em outras. As implicações organizacionais e gerenciais dessas duas teorias sugerem que MNEs que se formam para tanto resolver dificuldades transacionais quanto criar valor econômico enfrentarão desafios complicados ao tentar conciliar os imperativos organizacionais e gerenciais subentendidos por essas teorias. Este artigo conclui discutindo como MNEs podem lidar com esses conflitos organizacionais e gerenciais. Teece (2014) identifie deux théories de l'émergence des entreprises multinationales (Multinational Enterprises - MNEs) - l'une qui se concentre sur la manière dont les MNEs résolvent les difficultés transactionnelles pouvant apparaître dans les échanges sur le marché et l'autre qui se focalise sur la manière dont les MNEs facilitent la création de valeur économique qui est difficile à réaliser par le biais des échanges sur le marché - , et suggère que les deux théories sont importantes pour comprendre l'émergence des MNEs. Sont cependant très différentes les implications organisationnelles et managériales de ces deux théories. Les MNEs qui résolvent les difficultés transactionnelles sont généralement de nature hiérarchique, où les cadres supérieurs exercent un pouvoir de direction pour diriger leurs subordonnés, où les frontières de l'entreprise sont bien définies, et où le comportement des subordonnés est contrôlé afin de minimiser l'opportunisme. Les MNEs qui créent de la valeur économique sont généralement moins hiérarchisées, impliquent la création de relations de coopération entre les parties prenantes pour faciliter les investissements co-spécialisés, ont des frontières moins bien définies, et réduisent la menace de l'opportunisme en veillant à ce que les parties prenantes gagnent davantage dans la poursuite de cet échange que dans d’autres. Les implications organisationnelles et managériales de ces deux théories suggèrent que les MNEs qui se constituent à la fois pour résoudre des difficultés transactionnelles et pour créer de la valeur économique seront confrontées à des défis difficiles en essayant de concilier les impératifs organisationnels et managériaux qu'impliquent ces théories. Cet article conclut en examinant la manière dont les MNEs peuvent résoudre ces conflits organisationnels et managériaux. Markets efficiently coordinate economic activities, yet firms exist with complex structures. This paradox has intrigued scholars for decades. David Teece's research explores why multinational enterprises (MNEs) exist, focusing on two main theories. The first theory suggests that MNEs form to solve transactional problems, like shirking (avoiding responsibilities) or hold-ups (delays or obstacles), that markets cannot handle. The second theory argues that MNEs exist to leverage capabilities (unique skills or resources) and create value that markets cannot achieve. Teece highlights the need to balance these theories

Title: General manager succession dynamics in MNE foreign subsidiaries
Authors: Liang Li, Paul W. Beamish, Andreas P. J. Schotter
Abstract: La selección de sucesión de los gerentes generales de las filiales es un proceso critico en las empresas multinacionales. La investigación previa, fundamentada en el aprendizaje organizacional y las rutinas, ha encontrado que las dinámicas de sucesión del gerente general típicamente siguen ya se un ímpetu de aceleración o de desaceleración. Sin embargo, a medida que investigamos las heurísticas de la toma de decisiones de sucesión mediate entrevistas con gerentes de empresas multinacionales, observamos ni aceleración ni desaceleración. Por el contrario, encontramos algunas dinámicas consistentes de sucesión, algunas adoptando un enfoque basado en reglas con una dinámica corta de sucesión, otras adoptando un enfoque basado en metas con una dinámica de sucesión moderada, y otros adoptan un enfoque basado en personas con una dinámica larga de sucesión. Subyacente a estos modelos había una racionalidad limitada, una confiabilidad limitada y sus interacciones inesperadas. Nuestro estudio arroja luz sobre el papel critico de los gerentes generales en la gerencia de la sucesión, enriquece la teorización en Negocios Internacionales sobre el proceso de sucesión de la gerencia general en las filiales, y refina las condiciones límite del aprendizaje organizacional. El mensaje central es que solamente mirando las dinámicas de sucesión mediante unos lentes de aprendizaje organización puede correr el riesgo de pasar por lo alto mecanismos causales relevantes. Para que la teorización de las dinámicas de la gestión de filiales sea más fértil, el modelo comportamental debe de tener en cuenta las idiosincrasias de la toma de decisiones, así como también la heurística de los tomadores de decisión. Subsidiary general manager (GM) succession selection is a critical process in multinational enterprises (MNEs). Previous research, grounded in organizational learning and routines, has suggested that GM succession dynamics typically follow either an acceleration or a deceleration momentum. However, as we investigated succession decision-making heuristics through interviews with MNE managers, we observed neither acceleration nor deceleration. Instead, we found some consistent succession dynamics. Within this consistency, we found variations in decision-making models among subsidiaries—some adopting a rule-based approach with a short succession dynamic, some adopting a goal-based approach with a moderate succession dynamic, and others adopting a people-based approach with a long succession dynamic. Underlying these models were bounded rationality, bounded reliability, and their unexpected interactions. Our study sheds light on the critical role of managers in subsidiary management, enriches international business theorizing on the subsidiary GM succession process, and refines the boundary conditions of organizational learning. The central message is that looking solely at GM succession dynamics through an organizational learning lens may risk overlooking relevant causal mechanisms. To make the theorizing on the dynamics of subsidiary management more fertile, the behavioral model should account for the idiosyncrasies of decision-making as well as the heuristics of decision-makers. La sélection des successeurs des directeurs généraux ( General Manager —GM) de filiales est un processus essentiel dans les entreprises multinationales ( Multinational Enterprises —MNEs). Des recherches antérieures, fondées sur l'apprentissage organisationnel et les routines, ont suggéré que la dynamique de succession des GMs suit généralement un élan d'accélération ou de décélération. Cependant, lorsque nous avons étudié l'heuristique de prise de décision en matière de succession par le biais d'entretiens avec des dirigeants de MNEs, nous n'avons observé ni accélération ni décélération. Au contraire, nous avons constaté une certaine cohérence dans la dynamique de succession. Dans le cadre de cette cohérence, nous avons constaté des variations dans les modèles de prise de décisi

Title: Participation and upgrading along global value chains: the role of audit oversight
Authors: Sibo Liu, Lixin Su, Feng Wu, Xindong Zhu
Abstract: In recent years, the worldwide economy has become more intertwined through what are known as global value chains (GVCs – complex networks where production is divided across different countries, with each country specializing in certain stages of the manufacturing process). Information is vital in managing these GVCs, acting like a system that keeps the global network running smoothly. Auditing is a crucial institution in this context, as it guarantees the dependability of the financial information that companies use to make decisions and build trust with their partners. This research focuses on the effect of international inspections by the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB – a body established by the Sarbanes–Oxley Act in the United States, aiming to enhance the quality of audits for companies registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) – a federal agency responsible for enforcing federal securities laws and regulating the securities industry). Previous studies have shown that when the PCAOB inspects the auditors of foreign firms, the quality of these firms' financial reporting improves. This research uses a large dataset of U.S. waterway imports from international companies to analyze how these inspections affect GVC participation, particularly for firms exporting to the U.S. The study finds that after PCAOB inspections, there is a significant increase in exports from foreign firms to U.S. importers, especially in intermediate and capital goods. This suggests that better auditing leads to more trust and smoother cooperation within GVCs. The study also discovers that following inspections, the complexity of exported products increases, indicating a shift from generic to more specialized goods. These results are more pronounced for firms with lower initial reporting quality, smaller market shares, and those from countries with weaker institutions or higher geopolitical risks with the U.S. In conclusion, the research emphasizes the importance of auditing and reliable information in enhancing GVC participation and upgrading. It shows that PCAOB inspections not only improve financial reporting quality but also have a broader impact on international trade and the global economy. This has implications for policymakers and regulators, suggesting that supporting international audit oversight can have significant economic benefits. This text was initially drafted using artificial intelligence, then reviewed by the author(s) to ensure accuracy. Nous montrons que des normes d'audit partagées et améliorées, induites par la surveillance des audits découlant des inspections du Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) sur les auditeurs non américains, aident les entreprises exportatrices mondiales à se moderniser et à s'intégrer dans les chaînes de valeur mondiales (Global Value Chains - GVCs). À l'aide d'un ensemble de données sur les importations américaines par voie navigable en provenance de fournisseurs mondiaux de 36 pays, nous observons que les inspections internationales du PCAOB conduisent non seulement à une augmentation significative des exportations vers les acheteurs américains, en particulier pour les biens intermédiaires et d'équipement, mais aussi au fait que les exportateurs améliorent également la complexité de leurs produits. Ces résultats sont cohérents avec l'amélioration de la qualité de l'information des exportateurs et donc la réduction des frictions informationnelles avec les importateurs en aval. Faisant écho à cette notion, nous constatons que les inspections du PCAOB ont des impacts plus importants sur les GVCs pour les exportateurs confrontés à davantage de problèmes d'information, c'est-à-dire pour ceux dont la qualité des rapports ex ante est plus faible ou dont les parts de marché sont plus petites, et pour ceux qui sont situés dans des pays où les institutions sont plus faibles ou où le risque géopolitique avec les États-Unis est plus élevé. Title: Techno-nationalism and cross-border acquisitions in an age of geopolitical rivalry
Authors: Jing Li, Daniel M. Shapiro, Anastasia Ufimtseva, Peng Zhang
Abstract: Nous étudions la rivalité entre les États-Unis et la Chine dans le contexte du techno-nationalisme géopolitique, c'est-à-dire l'utilisation des politiques technologiques pour développer ou maintenir un avantage géopolitique. Nous appuyant sur la littérature des relations internationales, nous argumentons qu'un hégémon en place, lorsqu'il est menacé, cherche à maintenir l'équilibre du pouvoir par une combinaison de politiques intérieures et d'alliances extérieures. Nous examinons les impacts de deux politiques sur les acquisitions technologiques des entreprises chinoises : Le programme chinois Made in China 2025 (MIC2025), lancé en 2015, et la réponse des États-Unis en 2018 par le biais du Foreign Investment Risk Review Modernization Act (FIRRMA). Nous argumentons que le MIC2025 a encouragé les entreprises chinoises à acquérir des entreprises technologiques américaines, et que cela a été perçu comme une menace par les États-Unis, qui ont réagi en adoptant le FIRRMA pour limiter ces acquisitions. En utilisant les données d'acquisition de 2010 à 2022, nous constatons que le MIC2025 a augmenté les annonces d'acquisition des entreprises chinoises dans les secteurs technologiques critiques aux États-Unis, mais que le FIRRMA a eu un impact négatif à la fois sur les annonces et les réalisations. Nous trouvons également des preuves suggérant des effets de débordement du FIRRMA sur les pays alliés des États-Unis, mais seulement s'ils sont des leaders en matière d'innovation et peu dépendants de la Chine sur le plan commercial. Nous concluons que le techno-nationalisme géopolitique façonne les investissements transfrontaliers dans les technologies critiques, tant aux États-Unis que chez certains alliés. We study the U.S.–China rivalry in the context of geopolitical techno-nationalism, the use of technology policies to develop or maintain geopolitical advantage. We follow the international relations literature to argue that an incumbent hegemon, when threatened, seeks to maintain the balance of power through a combination of domestic policies and external alliances. We examine the effects of two policies on Chinese firms’ technology acquisitions: China’s Made in China 2025 (MIC2025), initiated in 2015, and the U.S. response in 2018 through the Foreign Investment Risk Review Modernization Act (FIRRMA). We argue that MIC2025 encouraged Chinese companies to acquire U.S. technology companies, and that this was perceived as a threat in the U.S., which countered through FIRRMA to limit such acquisitions. Using acquisition data from 2010 to 2022, we find that MIC2025 increased Chinese firms’ acquisition announcements in critical technology sectors in the U.S., but FIRRMA had a negative effect on both announcements and completions. We also find evidence suggesting spillover effects of FIRRMA to countries that are U.S. allies, but only if they are innovation leaders with low trade dependence on China. We conclude that geopolitical techno-nationalism shapes cross-border investments in critical technologies in both the U.S. and some allies. Estudamos a rivalidade entre EUA e China no contexto do tecno nacionalismo geopolítico, o uso de políticas sobre tecnologia para desenvolver ou manter vantagem geopolítica. Seguimos a literatura sobre relações internacionais para argumentar que uma hegemonia incumbente, quando ameaçada, busca manter o equilíbrio de forças por meio de uma combinação de políticas domésticas e alianças externas. Examinamos os efeitos de duas políticas nas aquisições de tecnologia de empresas chinesas: o Made in China 2025 (MIC2025), iniciado em 2015, e a resposta dos EUA em 2018 por meio da Lei de Modernização da Revisão de Risco de Investimento Estrangeiro (FIRRMA). Argumentamos que MIC2025 encorajou empresas chinesas a adquirir empresas de tecnologia dos EUA e que isso foi percebido como uma ameaça nos EUA, que contra-atacaram por meio da FIRRMA para limitar tais aquisições. Title: Industrial policy, green challenges, and international business
Authors: Gabriel R. G. Benito, Klaus E. Meyer
Abstract: Abstract Nation-states are designing their industrial policies increasingly to not only enhance national competitiveness, but also to simultaneously address “Green Challenges”, concerns about the natural environment that require concerted action among different actors in society, including domestic and foreign multinational enterprises (MNEs). This blending of global and national policy objectives is leading to a new wave of industrial policies in advanced economies that are informed by scholarly discourses in evolutionary economics, innovation systems, and 'wicked problems'. We discuss the implications of these sustainability-oriented industrial policies for MNEs. They operate in increasingly diverse local ecosystems shaped by local actors and local policies as we illustrate for two such ecosystems in Nordic countries: circular economy and energy transition. Many MNEs face a tension between capabilities they could use to help nations achieve their sustainability goals and incentives to protect existing rents and business models. They may thus engage pro-actively or reactively in both market and nonmarket realms in each country in which they operate. We discuss the interactions between MNEs, governments, and other actors in host countries pursuing both sustainability and competitiveness objectives, and outline how ensuing tensions create new challenges and opportunities for international business scholarship.

Title: Doing good for political gain: the instrumental use of the SDGs as nonmarket strategies
Authors: Christiaan Röell, Felix Arndt, Mirko H. Benischke, Rebecca Piekkari
Abstract: Abstract The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are changing the way multinational enterprises (MNEs) engage with host governments. The SDGs offer MNEs a unique opportunity to build political influence by assisting governments in attaining a host country’s social needs. However, international business scholars have largely remained silent on how MNEs strategize to repurpose ‘doing good’ into political influence. Based on a multiple case study of four Western European MNE subsidiaries in Indonesia, we uncover the strategies that MNEs use to turn their SDG initiatives into political access and influence. Our study reveals three nonmarket strategies – SDG-directed cross-sector partnership, SDG-directed conflict management, and SDG-directed constituency building. These actionable strategies help MNEs manage the tensions arising from misaligned government priorities, high levels of perceived corruption, and skepticism toward foreign firms. Our findings advance the literature on international nonmarket strategy by explaining how MNE subsidiaries resolve these tensions and convert SDG-directed investments into political access and influence without succumbing to locally institutionalized norms of corruption. Finally, our study suggests that emerging-market governments may benefit from rewarding MNEs for their investments that contribute to the SDGs, as long as they provide clear guidance and multi-stakeholder platforms that foster effective collaborations with MNEs.

Title: The interrelationships between corporate political activity and corporate environmental performance: the role of language diversity
Authors: Amir Shoham, Jedrzej George Frynas, Ahmad Arslan, Ofra Bazel-Shoham, Sang Mook Lee, Zaheer Khan, Shlomo Tarba
Abstract: Abstract Language affects almost every aspect of management in multinational enterprises (MNEs) but little is known about the impact of language on environmental performance. Our study investigates how language diversity affects the environmental performance of MNEs worldwide. We show that the grammatical structure of a language – specifically the first pronoun drop – is an important factor explaining the environmental performance of firms. Our analysis of 4454 company-year observations suggests that MNEs operating in societies that permit the first pronoun drop tend to have better environmental performance. Furthermore, we explore the impact of linguistic structure on the relationship between environmental performance and corporate political activity (CPA). We find that using the first pronoun drop of the local language moderates the influence of CPA on firms’ environmental performance. Our study concludes that international managers must pay greater attention to the neglected role of language in implementing environmental initiatives.

Title: Cross-border political ties: foreign firms’ campaign contributions and the crowding out of domestic competitors
Authors: Meghana Ayyagari, April Knill, Kelsey Syvrud
Abstract: Abstract A substantial body of literature has shown that political connections have benefited firms domestically, but their cross-border value for multinational enterprises (MNEs) remains understudied. This paper provides novel evidence on the strategic advantages MNEs gain through political ties in host countries and the consequences for domestic firms. Examining foreign companies’ contributions to US political campaigns through political action committees (PACs) sponsored by their US subsidiaries, we find that contributing foreign firms win significantly more U.S. government contracts than non-contributing foreign firms. Crucially, this increased access for foreign contributing firms crowds out government contract allocation to similar domestic firms that do not make political donations, even in regulated industries favoring domestic suppliers. Our findings demonstrate that MNEs can effectively leverage political connections as a non-market strategy to gain preferential treatment over local competitors in a host nation. However, these cross-border political ties come at the expense of domestic firms’ competitiveness, informing policy debates around restricting foreign corporate influence in domestic elections. From a managerial perspective, our findings suggest that strategic political ties are an important consideration for MNEs alongside traditional location factors when evaluating foreign investment decisions and navigating institutional complexities abroad.

Title: Exit, pursued by a bear! Global shocks and MNE responses
Perspectives on international business: insights from the JIBS Editors-in-Chief
Domestic financial conditions and MNCs’ global competitiveness: evidence from the Swiss franc shock
Authors: Christian Eufinger, Andrej Gill, Florian Hett
Abstract: In the complex realm of global commerce, multinational corporations (MNCs – companies that operate in more than one country) have a distinct benefit: they can access various financial markets globally to finance their activities. This capacity to obtain capital at more favorable rates can give them an edge over companies that only operate locally. However, the financial conditions in the country where an MNC is based can still have a significant impact. This research examines how the financial conditions at home can affect an MNC's global strategies and competitiveness. The study exploits a substantial policy shift in January 2015 by the Swiss National Bank (SNB – Switzerland's central bank). The SNB removed a limit on the Swiss franc's value against the euro, causing a sharp rise in the franc's value, and also reduced interest rates to −0.75%. This double shock offers a unique chance to observe how changes in a home country's financial conditions impact MNCs' investment and employment choices. The study utilized detailed company-level data from the Orbis database, comparing Swiss-based MNCs with their counterparts in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, and the Netherlands. The main findings were that Swiss MNCs capitalized on the lower interest rates and increased their debt financing, investments, and employment more than their European Union (EU – a political and economic union of 27European countries) counterparts. However, the stronger Swiss franc created a challenging environment for Swiss companies that heavily depended on exports, as their products became more costly abroad. Interestingly, the study discovered that the negative effects of the stronger Swiss franc were somewhat mitigated by the lower interest rates, suggesting that the SNB's policy helped alleviate potential downsides for Swiss MNCs. In conclusion, the research underscores the significance of an MNC's home-country financial conditions in shaping its global strategies. The ability to exploit favorable local financial conditions can provide MNCs with a significant advantage, influencing their investment and employment decisions. The study's insights are particularly pertinent for policymakers and business leaders, as they demonstrate how central bank policies can have extensive effects on the global competitiveness of MNCs. Title: Home country’s economic and political institutions: firms’ ownership decisions in cross-border acquisitions
Authors: Christine M. Chan, Lei Shi, Jingtao Yi
Abstract: Abstract The influences of a home country’s economic and political institutions on acquirers’ cross-border acquisitions (CBAs) ownership strategies remains unexplored. Acquirers face endogenous uncertainty (i.e., uncertainty that can be resolved in part by acquirers) when transferring headquarters resources to foreign target firms and exogenous uncertainty (i.e., uncertainty that cannot be resolved by acquirers) when there is an unpredictable policy change. We argue that well-developed economic and political institutions in a home country play a market-supporting and constraining role in mitigating endogenous and exogenous uncertainty respectively, enabling acquirers to seek high ownership stakes in CBAs. We also argue that the importance of a home country’s well-developed economic and political institutions for acquirers’ CBA ownership strategic decisions depends on mutual trade dependence between the acquirers’ home country and the target firms’ host countries and also on the economic capabilities of the acquirers developed in different industries and political capabilities developed in different host countries. To test these arguments, we analyze 133,623 CBAs between 2000 and 2020 and find support for the distinct roles played by a home country’s economic and political institutions.

Title: On the resilience of ESG firms during the COVID-19 crisis: evidence across countries and asset classes
Authors: Gianfranco Gianfrate, Mirco Rubin, Dario Ruzzi, Mathijs van Dijk
Abstract: We use the exogenous shock of COVID-19 to explore the resilience of firms with strong ESG (environmental, social, and governance) ratings across 63 countries and three asset classes: stocks, credit default swaps (CDS), and corporate bonds. We show that the resilience of strong ESG firms is not a consistent global phenomenon outside of North America and varies considerably across countries. Additional evidence points towards a substitution effect between firm-level sustainability performance as captured by ESG ratings and country-level sustainability performance especially in terms of healthcare coverage. Overall, our findings indicate that the capacity of strong ESG firms to serve as “rainy day assets” is geography-dependent and that ESG considerations can also affect international corporate debt markets. Mostramos que a resiliência de empresas boas em ESG não é um fenômeno global consistente fora da América do Norte e varia consideravelmente entre os países. Evidências adicionais apontam para um efeito de substituição entre o desempenho de sustentabilidade em nível de empresa, conforme capturado pelas classificações ESG e o desempenho de sustentabilidade em nível de país, especialmente em termos de cobertura de planos de saúde. No geral, nossas descobertas indicam que a capacidade de empresas boas em ESG de servir como "ativos para dias ruins" depende da geografia e que considerações ESG também podem afetar mercados internacionais de dívida corporativa. Title: Conceptualizing international new ventures as the nexus of entrepreneurship and international business
Authors: Shaker A. Zahra, Giuseppe Criaco, Olga Petricevic, Niron Hashai
Abstract: In the fast-paced world of global business, a special breed of companies known as international new ventures (INVs) has emerged. These firms begin their life with a global outlook, but research has often focused more on their international reach than on their entrepreneurial spirit. The study at hand seeks to fill this gap by exploring how the entrepreneurial behavior of INVs varies and how this affects their approach to foreign markets. The key finding is a new way of categorizing INVs that considers both their innovative behavior and their commitment to international markets. This study developed a typology (a system of classification) to better understand INVs. It looked at how these firms behave entrepreneurially – whether they make small changes to existing products, services, or business models (incremental entrepreneurship) or create entirely new markets with innovative offerings (radical entrepreneurship). The researchers also consider the firms' commitment to foreign markets, ranging from low to high. By combining these two dimensions, the study identified four distinct types of INVs. The research is based on a thorough review of existing literature and proposes a new perspective on how INVs operate. It is important because it helps us to understand the different capabilities and networks INVs use to innovate and expand internationally. The typology shows that not all INVs are the same. Some focus on making slight improvements to existing products, services, or business models and target specific foreign niches, while others aim to disrupt markets on a global scale with groundbreaking innovations. The study concludes that recognizing the diversity among INVs can lead to a better understanding of their strengths and how they can overcome challenges in international markets. This new classification system could help predict which INVs will be successful and guide future research into the unique capabilities and networks that different types of INVs develop. The potential impact of this research is significant. It offers a fresh lens through which policymakers, entrepreneurs, and scholars can view the international business landscape. By acknowledging the varied entrepreneurial approaches of INVs, we can better support these firms and foster innovation across borders. Looking ahead, this work could inspire new strategies for INVs to thrive in the global market and to contribute to the broader conversation on how entrepreneurship shapes international business. We propose a typology that captures the heterogeneity of international new ventures’ (INVs’) entrepreneurial behavior and their commitment to foreign markets. The typology identifies four types of INVs, highlighting the dynamic interplay between the degree of radicalness of their entrepreneurial behavior and the level of their foreign market commitment. By integrating theories from both international business and entrepreneurship, we illustrate how the diverse underlying capabilities and networks of different INV types provide strategic advantages. Moreover, we argue that changes in the degree of radicalness in INVs’ entrepreneurial behavior over time reveal important temporal dynamics with strategic and performance implications. Our typology addresses a limitation in international entrepreneurship research by emphasizing the INVs’ entrepreneurial essence, which has often been overlooked. Prior conceptualizations of INVs have primarily focused on aspects such as the degree and mode of internationalization, neglecting the diversity of their entrepreneurial approaches. Consequently, our understanding of the sources of INVs’ competitive advantage and resilience in international markets has been limited. Title: Foreign divestment: the missing piece in international business scholarship
Abstract: Abstract As international business (IB) scholars seek to invigorate the field and steer it away from what some deem a “research coma” resulting from a narrowing scope, the significance of foreign divestment (FD) has once again been relegated amidst other pressing topics. We advocate for elevating FD to the same level of importance as foreign direct investment (FDI). Despite emerging a decade after seminal contributions on FDI, FD has suffered from a notable lack of attention in IB research and educational curricula. However, FD, like FDI, is a common practice among firms and is gaining prominence in light of recent disruptions such as geopolitical conflicts, economic decoupling, digital transformation, and growing skepticism towards globalization. We identify two main setbacks to overcome: the persistent view of FD as merely a misstep in firms' internationalization strategies, and its perception as a subordinate aspect within broader themes of internationalization, including emerging topics such as deglobalization and decoupling. As we elaborate in this commentary, delving into FD at a more granular level can uncover disruptive spillovers that require pushing the boundaries of extant theorizing in IB; neglecting FD leaves the field incomplete and hampers its ability to fully grasp the complexities of global business dynamics.

Title: Globalization and stock price crash risk: evidence from the US granting permanent normal trade relations to China
Abstract: In recent years, the world has witnessed a significant rise in globalization (the process of interaction and integration among people, companies, and governments worldwide), which has greatly benefited the global economy. However, events like Brexit (the withdrawal of the United Kingdom from the European Union) and the US-China trade war (a conflict between the United States and China over trade policies) have sparked debates about the true costs and benefits of globalization. A pivotal moment in this ongoing process was China's entry into the World Trade Organization (WTO - an international organization that deals with the global rules of trade between nations), which marked a significant shift and led to a surge in globalization. This study concentrates on the effects of the China trade shock—specifically, the impact on financial stability in the US, as measured by stock price crash risk (the probability of a sudden and significant decrease in the price of a company's stock). The research investigates how the China trade shock, following the US granting Permanent Normal Trade Relations (PNTR - a legal designation in the United States for free trade with a foreign nation) status to China in 2000, affects the likelihood of sudden and significant stock price declines, known as stock price crashes. These crashes can have severe consequences, including the loss of investor wealth and potential financial crises. The study uses a quasi-natural experiment approach (a method used in social sciences to estimate causal relationships), leveraging the policy shock of PNTR, to identify the causal influence of the China trade shock on the stock price crash risk of US firms. The study analyzes extensive data on stock transactions and financial information from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP - a database of historical stock market data) and Compustat databases (a database of financial, statistical and market information on active and inactive global companies), covering the period from 1998 to 2003, with a total of 11,812 firm-year observations. The research is completed, and the findings show a significant decrease in stock price crash risk following the PNTR policy. This decrease is both statistically and economically meaningful, suggesting that globalization, through the China trade shock, can decrease the risk of stock price crashes for US firms. The results suggest that the China trade shock may discipline managers to avoid opportunistic behavior (actions taken to benefit oneself at the expense of others), which is a major contributor to stock price crashes. Additionally, the shock allows US firms to offshore production to China, taking advantage of lower labor costs, which could improve firm performance and reduce the likelihood of stock price crashes. In conclusion, the research uncovers a positive effect of the China trade shock on financial stability by reducing stock price crash risk. This finding contributes to the broader understanding of globalization's impact and suggests that the integration of China into the global trade system has benefits beyond economic growth, potentially leading to more stable financial markets. The study's insights could be valuable for investors, regulators, and policymakers as they navigate the complexities of globalization and its effects on financial stability.
